title: Information Technology and Society
body:
COMP 3309 asks what happens after software ships. Every other COMP course stops at whether a
program is correct, fast or maintainable. This one starts where those questions end, with a
system that works exactly as specified and changes somebody's life for the worse.

The course supplies frameworks for deciding whether a technology should be built, where every
other course asks whether it can be. Three ethical theories give three ways of arguing about
the same case, and they frequently disagree, which is the point: an argument that a decision is
right needs to name which standard it is right by. The rest of the course applies them to
automation, to privacy, to social media and to money.

It pairs with [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]], which asks how to build
the thing correctly, and with [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] and [[MACHINE LEARNING]],
which supply the systems this course examines most closely, since a model that decides who gets
a loan is making an ethical decision at scale whether or not anybody framed it that way.

## Topics

### Three ways to judge an action

[[Ethical Analysis]] is the skill the course tests: take a concrete case, apply each
framework, and say what each concludes and why. A framework is a standard for deciding, and the
three here disagree often enough that naming yours is required.

[[Utilitarianism]] judges an action by its consequences, choosing whatever produces the
greatest total wellbeing. It is the framework closest to how engineering decisions already get
made, since a cost-benefit analysis is a utilitarian calculation. Its difficulty is that totals
hide distribution, so an outcome that is excellent on average can be produced by imposing
severe harm on a small group.

[[Kantianism]] judges the action itself against a rule, asking whether the rule behind it could
be applied universally and whether it treats people as ends in themselves and never purely as
means. It produces firm answers where utilitarianism produces arithmetic, and it handles the
small-group problem directly, since using somebody as an instrument is prohibited regardless of
the total.

[[Social Contract Theory]] treats moral rules as an agreement rational people would
accept for mutual benefit. It is the framework that transfers best to a digital setting,
because a platform's terms of service, a privacy policy and a software licence are all
literally contracts, and the question becomes whether anyone could reasonably have agreed to
them.

The [[Trolley Problem]] is the standard vehicle for showing the disagreement, and its
technological form is concrete: an autonomous vehicle has to be programmed in advance for a
collision it cannot avoid, and that program is an ethical position written as code by somebody.

### Where reasoning goes wrong

[[Cognitive Bias]] covers the failures in reasoning that affect designers and users alike:
pattern matching that finds structure in noise, confirmation bias that weights supporting
evidence more heavily, and availability bias that mistakes memorability for frequency.

The course connects these to the statistical errors in [[STATISTICS]], since a false positive
is a Type I error and a false negative is a Type II error, and a system tuned to avoid one
necessarily produces more of the other. That trade is an ethical decision when the false
positive is a fraud alert on somebody's account and the false negative is a missed diagnosis.
Researcher bias is the same failure inside the process that measures a system's performance.

### Does technology shape society, or the reverse

Two positions frame the middle of the course, and they sit at opposite ends of a continuum and
the useful answers are usually between them.

[[Technological Determinism]] holds that technology develops by its own internal logic and
society adapts to it, so the printing press produced the Reformation and the mobile phone
produced the change in how people relate. It explains large historical shifts and treats the
technology as though nobody chose it.

[[Social Construction of Technology]] holds the reverse, that social groups
shape which technologies get built and which succeed. The design of a bicycle, the format of a
video cassette and the layout of a keyboard were settled by contests between groups with
different interests, and the winner was frequently the one with more influence.

Placing a specific technology on that continuum is the exercise, and the honest answer for most
is neither extreme.

### Social platforms

[[Social Media Dynamics]] covers what happens when a recommendation algorithm
optimises engagement. Engagement is measurable and correlates with content that provokes, so a
system scored on it amplifies outrage without anybody deciding to. That is the same failure
[[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] names when a reward function is optimised literally: the
system maximises the sentence that was written.

The consequences the course covers are the shape of public discourse under algorithmic sorting,
the formation of separate information environments, and the psychological effects of metrics
attached to social approval. [[The Metaverse]] extends the same questions to persistent
immersive spaces, where the platform owns the environment and identity, property and conduct
become design decisions.

### Work and money

[[Automation and Job Displacement]] is the economic core. Automation removes
tasks, and a job is a bundle of tasks, so the effect is uneven: work that is routine and
codifiable goes first, regardless of whether it is manual or cognitive. The historical pattern
is that total employment recovers and the distribution of it does not, so the people displaced
and the people who benefit are rarely the same people, which is a distribution problem
[[Utilitarianism]] handles poorly.

[[FinTech]] covers the same disruption applied to money, including digital payment, algorithmic
lending, crowdfunding and cryptocurrency. The recurring question is who is accountable when a
decision is automated, since a loan refused by a model has no author to appeal to.

### Privacy and data

[[Data Privacy]] is the legal block. The course separates the question of what is legal
from what people expect, because a policy nobody reads is consent in a legal sense and nothing
in a practical one. It covers data collection as a business model, the difference between data
volunteered and data inferred, and the fact that anonymised datasets can frequently be
re-identified by cross-referencing.

[[Surveillance]] covers the same capability exercised by institutions, along with the chilling
effect, where the knowledge of being observed changes behaviour whether or not anybody is
watching.

[[DIKW Hierarchy]] provides the vocabulary underneath both, separating data from
information, knowledge and wisdom. It is useful here because the debate frequently conflates
the levels: a system that collects vast data is not thereby producing knowledge, and the gap
between the levels is where most claims about what a dataset proves fall apart.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] (COMP 2633) asks how to build a system correctly.
  This course asks whether it should exist, and [[Project Success]] there is measured against
  a specification that this course examines.
- [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] supplies the systems most of the cases concern. The
  [[Rational Agent]] optimises a performance measure somebody wrote, and
  [[Reinforcement Learning]] shows what optimising the wrong one produces.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] supplies the [[Confusion Matrix]], where the choice between a
  [[False Positive]] and a [[False Negative]] is the trade this course treats as an ethical
  decision, and [[Stratification]] is one technical response to unequal error rates across
  groups.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) supplies [[Type I and Type II Errors]] and the
  [[Correlation]] warning that underlies most claims made from a dataset.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] (COMP 3612) builds the tracking infrastructure the privacy block
  discusses, in [[Cookies]], the [[Cookie Jar]] and [[HTTP-Only Cookies]].
- [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111) is the technical counterweight to [[Surveillance]], since
  encryption is what makes privacy enforceable by mathematics.
- [[HUMAN COMPUTER INTERACTION]] (COMP 3553) covers the design decisions this course
  evaluates, including the interfaces that shape what a user understands they are agreeing to.
- [[SYMBOLIC LOGIC]] (PHIL 1179) supplies the tools for evaluating an argument, and an ethical
  argument is [[Argument|an argument]] whose premises include a value.
